remediationRecommendation.error: Missing redo log files preventing database startup
remediationRecommendation.cause: Oracle database attempted to start but could not locate required redo log files (redo01.log, redo02.log, redo03.log) in the expected directory '/mnt/oradata/ORDBSDL/'. This typically occurs during database creation, restoration from backup, or when storage mount points are not properly configured. The 'No such file or directory' error indicates the files either don't exist or the mount path is inaccessible.
remediationRecommendation.context: 2025-02-20T04:37:30.060976+00:00 Database startup failed with ORA-00313: open failed for members of log group 1,2,3 of thread 1. Files not found: /mnt/oradata/ORDBSDL/redo01.log, redo02.log, redo03.log. Linux Error 2: No such file or directory occurred during database creation/startup sequence.
remediation: Verify FSx for NetApp ONTAP storage mount point '/mnt/oradata' is properly mounted and accessible
Check if redo log files exist in the correct location: ls -la /mnt/oradata/ORDBSDL/redo*.log
If files are missing, recreate redo logs: ALTER DATABASE ADD LOGFILE GROUP 1 '/mnt/oradata/ORDBSDL/redo01.log' SIZE 100M
Ensure proper file permissions for oracle user: chown oracle:oinstall /mnt/oradata/ORDBSDL/redo*.log
Verify storage connectivity and network paths to FSx for NetApp ONTAP
Check Oracle initialization parameter LOG_ARCHIVE_DEST settings
If performing database restoration, ensure all required files are restored including redo logs
Consider creating redo logs in multiple locations for redundancy
Monitor storage performance metrics to ensure adequate IOPS for redo log operations

remediationRecommendation.error: Control file I/O errors and corruption leading to instance termination
remediationRecommendation.cause: Severe I/O failures preventing Oracle from reading/writing control files located at '/mnt/oradata/ORDBSDL/control01.ctl' and '/mnt/oraredoctl/ORDBSDL/control02.ctl'. Multiple error types occurred: (1) Linux I/O Error 5 (Input/output error) indicating storage hardware/network issues, (2) Linux Error 96 (Protocol family not supported) suggesting network protocol configuration problems with FSx for NetApp ONTAP, and (3) Control file block corruption preventing critical database metadata updates. This cascaded into checkpoint process failures and ultimately instance termination.
remediationRecommendation.context: 2025-03-10T08:33:55.832730+00:00 to 2025-04-09T07:25:52.588099+00:00 Control file I/O errors escalated from file close failures (ORA-27045) to write errors (ORA-00206, ORA-00221) affecting both control01.ctl and control02.ctl. Linux errors included I/O failures and protocol family issues, indicating FSx storage connectivity problems. Checkpoint process (CKPT) terminated instance due to inability to maintain database consistency.
remediation: Immediately verify FSx for NetApp ONTAP storage connectivity and health status
Check network protocol configuration between Oracle server and FSx storage (NFS/iSCSI versions)
Restore control files from backup: RESTORE CONTROLFILE FROM '/backup/location/control.bkp'
Recreate control file if restoration fails: CREATE CONTROLFILE REUSE SET DATABASE
Verify mount points are accessible: ls -la /mnt/oradata /mnt/oraredoctl
Check file system integrity: fsck on mounted volumes if safe to do so
Monitor FSx performance metrics for latency, IOPS, and throughput issues
Ensure redundant network paths to storage are configured and functional
Implement control file multiplexing across different storage locations
Enable Oracle block corruption detection and automatic repair features
Review Oracle alert logs and FSx CloudWatch metrics during incident timeframe
Consider upgrading to Oracle Managed Files (OMF) for better file management

remediationRecommendation.error: Instance termination due to critical errors
remediationRecommendation.cause: Oracle database instances underwent emergency shutdown due to critical errors that compromised database integrity. The termination was initiated by various Oracle background processes (CKPT, USER processes) when they encountered unrecoverable errors such as control file corruption, I/O failures, or other system-level issues. This represents the final stage of error escalation where Oracle determines the instance cannot safely continue operation.
remediationRecommendation.context: Instance termination events occurred following critical errors. Sequence: 2025-02-20T04:36:51.129751+00:00 Instance abort (OS id: 22947) followed by restart, and 2025-03-10T08:33:57.419549+00:00 termination due to ORA errors after control file failures.
remediation: Review Oracle diagnostic dumps and incident files for root cause analysis
Check system state dump files in $ORACLE_BASE/diag/rdbms/ordbsdl/ordbsdl/trace/
Verify storage subsystem health and connectivity to FSx for NetApp ONTAP
Restart Oracle instance after resolving underlying storage/network issues
Implement Oracle High Availability solutions (RAC, Data Guard) to prevent single points of failure
Enable automatic diagnostic repository (ADR) for better incident tracking
Configure Oracle Enterprise Manager or CloudWatch for proactive monitoring
Review and tune Oracle parameters related to error handling and recovery
Establish regular backup and recovery testing procedures

remediationRecommendation.error: Empty temporary tablespace after database creation
remediationRecommendation.cause: Temporary tablespace 'TEMP' was created without any tempfiles during database creation or restoration process. This commonly occurs when using backup control files or when the CREATE DATABASE command doesn't specify a default temporary tablespace. While not immediately critical, this can impact sort operations, temporary table creation, and overall database performance.
remediationRecommendation.context: 2025-02-20T04:37:33.886013+00:00 Empty temporary tablespace TEMP detected after database creation. Recommendation provided to add tempfiles using ALTER TABLESPACE command.
remediation: Add tempfile to TEMP tablespace: ALTER TABLESPACE TEMP ADD TEMPFILE '/mnt/oradata/ORDBSDL/temp01.dbf' SIZE 1G AUTOEXTEND ON
Verify temporary tablespace is set as default: ALTER DATABASE DEFAULT TEMPORARY TABLESPACE TEMP
Check available space in FSx for NetApp ONTAP volume before creating tempfiles
Monitor temporary tablespace usage and configure appropriate autoextend settings
Consider creating multiple tempfiles for better I/O distribution

remediationRecommendation.cause: Files exist in the db_recovery_file_dest location that are not registered in Oracle's recovery catalog. This typically occurs after control file restoration, standby database setup, or when the recovery file destination was previously enabled and disabled. These orphaned files can consume space and may interfere with backup operations.
remediationRecommendation.context: 2025-02-20T04:37:33.886013+00:00 Files exist in db_recovery_file_dest that are unknown to database. Caused by backup controlfile restoration or recovery area configuration changes.
remediation: Catalog existing recovery files: RMAN> CATALOG RECOVERY AREA
Review files in recovery destination: ls -la $ORACLE_BASE/fast_recovery_area/
Remove unneeded files manually if they cannot be cataloged
Verify db_recovery_file_dest parameter setting: SHOW PARAMETER db_recovery_file_dest
Ensure adequate space in FSx for NetApp ONTAP volume for recovery operations
Configure RMAN retention policy appropriately for your backup strategy

remediationRecommendation.cause: Oracle Advanced Queuing (AQ) is not properly configured with AQ_TM_PROCESSES set to 0 and no enabled queues. This disables the AQ time manager and can impact applications that rely on message queuing functionality. While not critical for basic database operations, it may affect specific application features that use Oracle's messaging capabilities.
remediationRecommendation.context: 2025-02-20T04:40:13.474490+00:00 AQ_TM_PROCESSES=0 and no enabled queues detected. Advanced Queuing time manager not started, potentially affecting queue-dependent applications.
remediation: Configure AQ time manager: ALTER SYSTEM SET AQ_TM_PROCESSES=1
Enable queues if needed by applications: BEGIN DBMS_AQADM.START_QUEUE('queue_name'); END;
Review application requirements for Advanced Queuing functionality
Monitor queue performance if AQ is enabled for production use
Document AQ configuration requirements for future database deployments

remediationRecommendation.cause: Heavy memory swapping detected on the Oracle database server, indicating insufficient physical RAM for the current workload. Excessive swapping can lead to significant performance degradation, I/O timeouts, and potential instance eviction in cloud environments. This suggests the server may be undersized for the Oracle SGA and PGA memory requirements.
remediationRecommendation.context: 2025-04-24T09:31:45.822489+00:00 Heavy swapping observed, leading to potential timeouts and performance issues. System resource constraints affecting Oracle database performance.
remediation: Increase EC2 instance memory or upgrade to memory-optimized instance type
Tune Oracle SGA and PGA parameters to fit available physical memory
Review Oracle memory parameters: SHOW PARAMETER sga_target, pga_aggregate_target
Monitor system memory usage: vmstat, free -h, and CloudWatch memory metrics
Consider enabling Oracle Automatic Memory Management (AMM) or ASMM
Optimize application queries to reduce memory consumption
Implement connection pooling to reduce memory overhead per session

remediationRecommendation.cause: Oracle detected a deadlock situation where two or more transactions were waiting for each other to release locks, creating a circular dependency. This is typically caused by applications accessing resources in different orders or inefficient SQL design. While Oracle automatically resolves deadlocks by rolling back one transaction, frequent deadlocks can indicate application design issues.
remediationRecommendation.context: 2025-09-15T05:54:31.699700+00:00 Deadlock detected with detailed information available in trace file. Automatic deadlock resolution performed by Oracle.
remediation: Review deadlock trace file for detailed analysis: /u01/app/oracle/diag/rdbms/ordbsdl/ordbsdl/trace/ordbsdl_ora_1182122.trc
Analyze application code to ensure consistent resource ordering
Implement proper exception handling for deadlock scenarios in applications
Consider reducing transaction scope and duration
Use appropriate locking strategies (SELECT FOR UPDATE with NOWAIT)
Monitor deadlock frequency using AWR reports
Review and optimize SQL statements causing high contention

remediationRecommendation.error: ORA-15173: entry 'orapwasm' does not exist in directory '/'
remediationRecommendation.cause: The ASM (Automatic Storage Management) instance is unable to locate the ASM password file 'orapwasm' in the root directory. This occurs when ASM is configured to use password file authentication but the password file is missing, corrupted, or located in an incorrect directory. This is a common issue during ASM setup or after configuration changes.
remediationRecommendation.context: 2025-09-17T04:11:20.272399+00:00 ERROR Errors in file /u01/app/grid/diag/asm/+asm/+ASM/trace/+ASM_ora_49893.trc: ORA-15173: entry 'orapwasm' does not exist in directory '/' followed by instance termination sequence. ASM was attempting to mount disk groups DATA, DATADG, DATAAG, DATARG with external redundancy when the error occurred.
remediation: Create the ASM password file using orapwd utility: orapwd file=$ORACLE_HOME/dbs/orapwASM password=<sys_password> entries=10
Verify the ASM_DISKSTRING parameter is correctly set to point to your disk devices (currently set to 'ORCL:*')
Check the REMOTE_LOGIN_PASSWORDFILE parameter in ASM spfile - it should be set to 'EXCLUSIVE' for single-instance ASM
Ensure the oracle user has proper read/write permissions on the ASM password file location
Verify that the ASM disk groups (DATA, DATADG, DATAAG, DATARG) are properly configured and accessible
Check if the underlying storage devices mapped to ORCL:DISK1-5 are available and not experiencing I/O issues
Review FSx for NetApp ONTAP storage connectivity and ensure iSCSI/NFS mounts are stable
Examine the complete ASM alert log for any preceding storage-related errors that might have caused the password file to become inaccessible
Consider recreating the ASM instance configuration if the password file corruption persists

remediationRecommendation.error: ASM instance termination due to missing password file
remediationRecommendation.cause: The ASM instance underwent an abnormal shutdown (abort) triggered by the missing ASM password file error (ORA-15173). The instance termination sequence shows USER process (ospid: 49883) initiated the shutdown, followed by ORA-1092 (opitsk aborting process). This indicates a cascading failure where the password file authentication failure led to process termination and ultimately instance shutdown.
remediationRecommendation.context: 2025-09-17T04:11:21.846005+00:00 ERROR Shutting down ORACLE instance (abort) (OS id: 49883) followed by USER (ospid: 49883): terminating the instance and ORA-1092 : opitsk aborting process. The shutdown sequence occurred after ASM failed to authenticate due to missing password file, affecting disk groups DATA, DATADG, DATAAG, DATARG operations.
remediation: Immediately recreate the ASM password file: orapwd file=$ORACLE_HOME/dbs/orapwASM password=<sys_password>
Restart the ASM instance after password file creation: srvctl start asm
Verify all ASM disk groups mount successfully after restart
Check the underlying storage connectivity to FSx for NetApp ONTAP volumes
Ensure the ASM disk devices (ORCL:DISK1-5) are properly configured and accessible
Review storage performance metrics during the incident to rule out I/O timeout issues
Implement monitoring for ASM password file existence to prevent future occurrences
Consider setting up ASM password file backup and recovery procedures
Validate that all dependent Oracle database instances can reconnect to ASM after restart
